prompt.context: Our client, the Toto Foundation, is a new non-profit arm of a well-known drone manufacturing and logistics company that is exploring aid projects in Africa. Our client is seeking your expertise to determine where and how to deploy their technology to have the maximum impact.
prompt.question: Determine where and how the Toto Foundation should deploy their drone technology in Africa to have the maximum impact on human lives while staying within budget.

clarifying_info.q: What does the parent company do?
clarifying_info.a: The parent company manufactures and sells drones. They have extensive commercial experience in the US, primarily in transportation of light packages and limited military/defense applications.
The foundation has a $4 million upfront grant and $1 million per year thereafter. There are no additional sources of funding.

clarifying_info.q: What are the project goals and constraints?
clarifying_info.a: Maximize impact on human lives while staying within budget. Safety is the primary concern. The grant can only apply to projects in Africa. Success of this phase will prompt future investment.

exhibits.title: Project Proposals
exhibits.shows: A table comparing six potential drone aid projects across four dimensions: Expertise (1-5), Need (1-5), Impact relative to existing solutions (1-5), and Upfront Deployment Cost.

exhibits.title: Target Country Data
exhibits.shows: A table with population, density, and country size for 5 African countries, plus a radar/spider chart comparing all 5 countries on 5 dimensions: Ease of Doing Business, Vaccination Rate (%), Poverty Level, Danger to Nonprofits, and Quality of Road Infrastructure. Higher bar = higher score on each dimension.

data.radar_chart_note: Rwanda has relatively high vaccination rates and road quality; Tanzania has high danger to nonprofits; Senegal and Guinea show lower vaccination rates and lower danger to workers; Central African Republic shows high need but high danger and low ease of doing business.

exhibits.title: Annual Cost Calculation Inputs
exhibits.shows: A table providing operational parameters for Senegal and Guinea: vials per flight, miles per delivery (roundtrip), fuel and maintenance cost per mile, days of flying per year, total flights per day, and annual regulatory and ground facility costs. Additional notes state drone costs are already in upfront development costs and a biotech firm is donating all vaccines and medication.

notes: Drone costs included in upfront development costs
Biotech firm donates vaccines and medication — no product cost

framework: Existing Capabilities: drone capabilities, deployment expertise, and available funding ($4M upfront, $1M/year)
Priorities: lives impacted, budget limitations (upfront and ongoing)
Personnel/Firm: existing partnerships that can be leveraged
Target Market: identify needs — food, medicine, agriculture, security — and how well they match drone capabilities
Trends: political instability, what needs are already being met by others
Other Considerations: infrastructure available, regulatory approval, safety and flight risks

questions.prompt: Question 1: Based on your analysis, which of the six proposed projects is most attractive for the foundation to pursue?
questions.guidance: Step 1 — eliminate on budget: Blood & Plasma Delivery ($11.5M upfront) and Insulin Delivery ($6.5M upfront) both exceed the $4M upfront grant and must be eliminated. Step 2 — eliminate on expertise: Crop Monitoring and Poacher Monitoring both score 1 on expertise, signaling serious operational risk; eliminate them. Step 3 — compare survivors: Dry Food Delivery (expertise 4, need 3, impact 2, $3.7M) vs. Vaccine & General Medicinal Delivery (expertise 4, need 5, impact 5, $3.8M). Both have similar expertise scores and upfront costs, but Vaccine & General Medicinal Delivery dominates on need and impact. Select Vaccine & General Medicinal Delivery. Strong candidates will add qualitative insight: vaccines are light and easy to transport, simple to administer, and address a critical gap in developing countries. Risks include temperature sensitivity, supply chain fragility, and potential shortages.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What factors should the client consider when choosing a launch country, and which two of the five candidate countries should they select?
questions.guidance: Brainstorm first (before Exhibit 2 is shown). Good candidates list relevant criteria: country size, population, demographics. Great candidates categorize: (1) Population/Demographics — density (drones add value in low-density areas where roads are poor), total population large enough to support investment, age/disease profile; (2) Health/Medical — vaccination rate (most benefit in low-vaccinated areas), deaths from preventable diseases; (3) Safety/Other — danger to nonprofit workers, ease of doing business, road infrastructure quality. After brainstorm, provide Exhibit 2. Apply framework to eliminate: Rwanda has relatively high vaccination rates and good road quality paired with lower poverty — already well-served, lower marginal impact. Tanzania has high need but also high danger to nonprofit workers. Central African Republic has high need but high danger and very low ease of doing business. The two selected countries are Senegal and Guinea: both have lower vaccination rates, lower poverty-adjusted road quality, and low danger to workers, making them high-need and operationally feasible.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Math): Calculate annual costs and impact (vials delivered per year) for both Senegal and Guinea.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute total annual flight cost and total vials delivered for each country. Both countries come in at exactly $1M/year, matching the annual grant. Great candidates note that Senegal's lower variable cost per flight allows easier scalability. Senegal delivers more than double the medicine per year (300,000 vs. 120,000 vials) for the same cost, making it the superior choice.

math.setup: For each country: Fuel & Maintenance Cost/Flight = Miles/Flight x Cost/Mile. Total Cost/Day = Flights/Day x Cost/Flight. Annual Flight Cost = Total Cost/Day x 300 days. Total Annual Cost = Annual Flight Cost + Regulatory & Ground Cost. Vials/Year = Vials/Flight x Flights/Day x 300 days.
steps: Senegal — Vials/Year: 100 vials x 10 flights x 300 days = 300,000 vials
Guinea — Vials/Year: 80 vials x 5 flights x 300 days = 120,000 vials
math.answer: Senegal: $1,000,000/year cost, 300,000 vials delivered. Guinea: $1,000,000/year cost, 120,000 vials delivered. Both fit the annual budget, but Senegal delivers 2.5x more medicine per dollar.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the Toto Foundation consider when selecting a target country for vaccine and general medicinal drone delivery?

categories.name: Population & Demographics
ideas: Population density — drones add most value in low-density areas where road access is poor
Total population — large enough to justify investment
Age profile and disease burden — certain populations more susceptible to vaccine-preventable diseases

categories.name: Health & Medical Need
ideas: Current vaccination rate — most impact in low-vaccinated areas
Deaths from preventable diseases — higher burden = greater potential lives saved
Availability of existing health delivery infrastructure

categories.name: Safety & Operational Feasibility
ideas: Danger to nonprofit field workers and volunteers
Ease of doing business and government cooperation
Quality of road and ground infrastructure for last-mile support

categories.name: Strategic & Financial
ideas: Country size and geographic dispersion of population
Political stability and risk of policy reversal
Existing partnerships or NGOs already operating in country
Potential for future scale-up if pilot succeeds

recommendation: Launch the Vaccine & General Medicinal Delivery program in Senegal

Senegal offers high need (low vaccination rates), low operational risk (low danger to workers, acceptable ease of doing business), and the highest delivery impact — 300,000 vials per year at the same $1M annual cost as Guinea, which delivers only 120,000 vials
risks: This is the foundation's first international drone project — operational unknowns are significant
The vaccine partnership with the biotech firm is untested; supply reliability is uncertain
Regulatory environment for drone flights could change
Political instability could shift needs rapidly or disrupt operations
Infrastructure for administering vaccines at the point of delivery may be inadequate
next_steps: Launch a pilot program to confirm that actual costs align with the estimates in Exhibit 3
Explore complementary infrastructure projects to build out drone delivery capacity (noting these are outside the current budget scope)
Begin obtaining regulatory approvals and expand the partnership network (biotech, local NGOs, governments)
Establish a detailed rollout timeline and success metrics tied to lives impacted
